title: the summit sit
hook: a lotus leaf sits in the pond all day, and the water rolls off it in beads
carry: water sliding from a lotus leaf

segments.voice: Yesterday, the modern teachers, and Ramana's question: to whom did this thought come? Today, the three tracks.

Rain falls on a pond. The water gathers on a lotus leaf in bright beads, rolls to the edge, and slides off. The leaf has been in the water all its life. It isn't wet. The Bhagavad Gita uses that leaf in its fifth chapter, as a picture of someone who acts fully in the world and isn't stained by it. That chapter sat inside the lineage weeks of this year, when the path split into three tracks: karma, bhakti and jnana.
screen: `WATER ON A LOTUS LEAF.` → `IN THE POND, NOT WET.` → `THE THREE TRACKS.`

segments.voice: Here is the Gita's line, in paraphrase: one who acts while placing every action in Brahman, letting go of clinging, is not touched by wrong, as a lotus leaf is not touched by water. Hold that leaf up to each of the year's three tracks. The karma track read Gita chapters three, four and five, and designed a year of service. There the leaf means doing the work well and setting down the result. The bhakti track read the Gita Govinda and the Bhagavata's tenth book, and sang kirtan. There the leaf turns into an offering. Elsewhere the Gita has Krishna say, in paraphrase: whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you give, do it as an offering to me. The act is the same. Now it is a gift. The jnana track read Shankara's Crest-Jewel of Discrimination and the Ashtavakra Gita. There the leaf is the witness. Ashtavakra tells King Janaka, in paraphrase: you are not earth, water, fire, air or space; know yourself as the witness of all these. The water rolls by; the one who sees it was never wet. Three tracks, three readings of one leaf. And the Gita itself, in the same chapter, says that only the childish call the path of knowledge and the path of action different; the one who truly stands in either reaches the fruit of both. Read that way, the tracks aren't a contest. They're three ways up.
screen: `NOT TOUCHED, LIKE A LOTUS LEAF.` · `KARMA: SET DOWN THE RESULT.` · `BHAKTI: MAKE IT AN OFFERING.` · `JNANA: THE WITNESS, NEVER WET.` · then, large: `THREE WAYS UP.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one ordinary task from today, a dish, an email, a drive, and hold it for a few breaths the karma way: done well, the result let go. Then the bhakti way: if you pray, see it as something offered. Then the jnana way: notice the one who watches it being done, still and dry like the leaf, and don't pick a favorite.
Padma-patra. The lotus leaf, sitting in water all its life and never wet, the Gita's picture for the three tracks of karma, bhakti and jnana.
Your line: water sliding from a lotus leaf. Tomorrow, a shelf of practices. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: The paths of karma, bhakti and jnana are walked side by side and in combination: selfless work and service, devotion in worship and kirtan, and study and inquiry with a teacher; the Gita is read as holding all three.

fork.setup: you've finished a piece of work and done it well. the result is out of your hands. what does the Gita's lotus leaf picture suggest?
options: hold on tight until the result comes in.
act fully, then let the result roll off, like water on a leaf.
next time, don't act at all.
fork.reveal: the Gita pictures someone who acts, places the action in Brahman and lets go of clinging, untouched as a lotus leaf by water. it never says to stop acting.

what a scholar hears: Gita 5.4–5 and 5.10, padmapatram ivambhasa, like a lotus leaf by water.

chat.says: How can someone work hard in the world and not get stained by it?
options: Like a lotus leaf in water: act fully, but let go of clinging.
By working only on tasks that are already pure and holy.
By never caring whether the work is done well or badly.
chat.meaning: Gita 5.10: one who acts, placing actions in Brahman and letting go of clinging, is untouched, as a lotus leaf by water.

notes: Fifth summit sit (1047–1053): revisits the lineage track (964–1005): karma (Gita 3–5, a year of service), bhakti (Gita Govinda, Bhagavata 10, kirtan), jnana (Vivekachudamani, Ashtavakra Gita). 'Crest-Jewel of Discrimination' is used for Vivekachudamani; confirm the English title.

Paraphrases: Gita 5.10 (brahmany adhaya karmani sangam tyaktva karoti yah, lipyate na sa papena padmapatram ivambhasa); 9.27 (whatever you do, eat, offer, give, do it as an offering to me); 5.4–5 (only children, not the wise, speak of Samkhya and Yoga as different). Note Gita 5.2 also says karma yoga excels renunciation of action; the script doesn't raise that, to keep to 5.4–5. Check.
Ashtavakra Gita 1.3 paraphrase (you are not earth, water, fire, air or space; know yourself as the witness of these, as consciousness). Confirm verse number.
Arnold's Song Celestial (1885) is on the validator list, but the writer isn't certain of its exact wording for these verses, so nothing is quoted.
